# Horizon Horizon is Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 rewritten in Rust: a native game that reads the same worlds, follows the same rules and generates the same terrain as the Java game, and is checked against it by 281 differential harnesses. You play it through a small launcher, on the files from your own copy of Minecraft. It is free, open source and unofficial. > Not an official Minecraft product. Not approved by or associated with Mojang or Microsoft. Horizon contains no Minecraft code, assets or data: you need your own legally obtained copy of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3. ## Download Horizon is installed through **the Horizon launcher**. Get it from [playhorizon.dev](https://playhorizon.dev) (the Download button picks your system) or from [the launcher releases](https://github.com/horizon-rust/horizon/releases?q=launcher-v&expanded=true), for Linux x86-64, macOS on Apple Silicon or Windows x64. The launcher installs and updates the game, prepares its files from your own copy of Minecraft, and updates itself. **You need** a Microsoft account that owns Minecraft: Java Edition (the launcher signs in with it, as other launchers do; see [Microsoft account](docs/microsoft-account.md)); Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3, played once (the official launcher, Prism, MultiMC and other launchers all work); a Java 25 runtime, for the one-time preparation; and a GPU with Vulkan on Linux and Windows, or any Apple Silicon Mac. Step by step, with macOS's first-open prompt and the first launch: [Install and first launch](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/install).
## What works today The [documentation](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/) covers each of these. - **The game:** singleplayer with vanilla's world generation, mobs, villagers, raids, redstone, every command, the HUD and the recipe book, on saves in vanilla's format. Worlds from 1.8 to 26.2 are upgraded as vanilla does. [Status table](#project-status). - **Horizon's own extras:** new menus (vanilla's are one setting away), graphics presets, distant terrain up to 1024 chunks, controller support, optional zoom, minimap and more, all off by default where they would change the vanilla look. See [Settings](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/settings). - **Resource packs and data packs:** resource packs work, and data packs load functions, predicates and item modifiers. - **Playing with others:** invite friends from the pause menu's Friends button with a code, Open to LAN, and joining servers, online-mode ones with the Microsoft account the launcher signs in with. See [Multiplayer](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/multiplayer). - **Mods:** Horizon has its own mod system (Rust compiled to WebAssembly). Java mod jars do not run. See [Mods and data packs](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/mods). Screenshots, captured in the Rust client itself with vanilla assets and no mods or shaders:
## Host a server The launcher's **Servers** page creates, starts, backs up and updates a Horizon server with buttons, and invites friends over Tailscale. On a VPS, `horizon-server` installs with one command and runs without Java. Guide: [Host a server](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/hosting) ([reference](docs/hosting.md)). ## Modpacks The launcher's **Modpacks** page imports a Modrinth or CurseForge pack, shows which of its mods Horizon can carry over, and plays the ones it can as their own profile. Today that means content mods made of data and assets; mods with Java code are not ported yet. See [Modpacks](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/modpacks). ## Agent control AI agents and scripts can play Horizon. `horizon-ctl`, shipped beside the game in every release folder, is a command line that reads the game as JSON and acts like a player; `horizon-ctl mcp` serves the same commands as an MCP server (one tool per command, screenshots returned as images). ```sh horizon-ctl launch --world Survival --seed 5 --wait # finds the version the launcher installed horizon-ctl state # position, health, food, target, screen... horizon-ctl find-block birch_log # the nearest logs horizon-ctl goto -0.5 65 -2.5 --near 2.5 # walks there along a path horizon-ctl break -1 65 -3 # mines it; replies with the drops horizon-ctl open-inventory && horizon-ctl click-slot 0 # menus: slots, buttons by label, text fields ``` Commands block until the action is done and reply with what happened; errors are JSON with distinct exit codes, `horizon-ctl help` lists every command and `horizon-ctl COMMAND --help` explains one with examples. It talks to the game over a Unix socket on Linux and macOS and over a token-protected localhost port on Windows. See [Agent control in the native client guide](docs/native-client.md#agent-control-horizon-ctl-and-mcp). ## Build from source For developers. Requirements: Rust 1.90 or newer, Python 3.10 or newer, JDK 25, and on Linux the ALSA and udev development headers (`libasound2-dev libudev-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu). Development and the vanilla harnesses run on Linux. Horizon contains no game files and never downloads them. It builds its resources from **your own copy** of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3, verified against the checksums in `research-lock.json`: 1. **Client:** install Java Edition with the official launcher and play 26.3 once. Horizon reads `versions/26.3/`, `libraries/` and `assets/` from the launcher's game directory (`~/.minecraft` on Linux). If yours lives elsewhere, pass `--minecraft-dir` or set `HORIZON_MINECRAFT_DIR`. 2. **Server jar:** the 26.3 server jar, from the `downloads.server.url` in your launcher's `versions/26.3/26.3.json` (or [minecraft.net/download/server](https:/

### Critical requirements before implementation

1. **Prove Android feasibility first.** Inspect the actual Horizon checkout, Cargo workspace, client entry point, rendering architecture, platform-specific dependencies, window/event handling, audio backend and filesystem assumptions. Do not assume that a Gradle wrapper or successful Rust cross-compilation means the game works on Android.
2. **Create a minimal working prototype.** Target `aarch64-linux-android` first, subject to dependency compatibility. Use the Android NDK to attempt a real client build. Verify the Android surface lifecycle and GPU rendering with a minimal wgpu/winit prototype before attempting a full port. Document every blocker and its proposed fix.
3. **Define the resource-import workflow.** Determine exactly how users prepare and import the required Minecraft resources using their own legally obtained game files. Never bundle Minecraft's proprietary game assets or server JAR in the APK. Do not assume that the existing desktop preparation workflow works on Android.
4. **Implement in milestones.**

- Milestone A: launch an Android APK and render a frame on a real device.
- Milestone B: start Horizon and enter a local single-player world using imported resources.
- Milestone C: implement touchscreen controls, keyboard/gamepad support where feasible, audio and suspend/resume.
- Milestone D: add Microsoft authentication by adapting Horizon's existing account implementation where possible, followed by secure credential storage and explicit offline-profile semantics.
- Milestone E: validate the debug APK on physical Android hardware and document remaining limitations.
5. **Choose the native integration explicitly.** Decide whether Horizon will run through an Android-compatible native application entry point or a JNI-based integration. Document how the Android surface, rendering loop, lifecycle events, input events, logging and shutdown reach the Rust client. Do not merely launch the desktop executable from Java.
6. **Protect the existing repository state.** Inspect `git status` and preserve all pre-existing changes. The reported 3,414 deleted tracked files must not be restored or removed without understanding why they are missing. Never use destructive Git cleanup or reset commands to make the working tree appear clean.
7. **Report evidence, not assumptions.** For each milestone, provide changed files, exact build commands, build results, test results and known blockers. Never claim that gameplay works unless a world has actually been entered and tested.
The first objective is a reproducible Android build that renders Horizon, not a complete launcher with authentication and every feature. Do not begin large-scale implementation until the first Android rendering prototype has established that the architecture is viable.

 # Horizon for Android MVP
 
 ## Problem and proposed approach
 
 Horizon is a native Rust Minecraft Java Edition implementation, while PojavLauncher is an Android launcher for Java-based Minecraft. The Android MVP will adapt PojavLauncher’s Android application shell and reusable Android input/storage patterns, but run Horizon’s Rust client rather than bundling a Java runtime or invoking Pojav’s Minecraft/LWJGL pipeline. Build a single end-to-end Android path: install and start Horizon, sign in with Microsoft or choose a standalone offline identity, enter a world, and play with touchscreen controls.
 
 Reuse Pojav code only after checking each reused component’s license and dependencies. Keep required notices and source availability; do not carry over unrelated game binaries/assets or imply that Pojav code is Horizon code. Keep the existing root-level deletions untouched and work in `horizon/` and `PojavLauncher/`.
 
 ## Scope and todos
 
 1. **Map the Android integration boundary.** Confirm Rust Android target/build support, `winit`/`wgpu` lifecycle and rendering requirements, desktop-only launcher assumptions, Pojav activity/input/storage components, and per-component licensing. Decide the supported Android API level and initial ABI based on what builds and runs.
 2. **Create the Android application and Rust client bridge.** Adapt the Pojav Android Gradle application into a Horizon-branded shell, remove irrelevant Java-game/JRE launch paths from the MVP, cross-compile Horizon for Android, and connect Android lifecycle, display surface, logs, and game start/stop to the Rust client. Preserve a clear error path for unsupported GPUs, missing resources, or failed startup.
 3. **Implement Android account selection and persistence.** Provide Microsoft sign-in using an appropriate supported flow and protect refresh/session credentials with Android secure storage. Add the requested standalone offline profile with a validated player name and no Microsoft ownership prerequisite. Pass session data to the client without putting secrets in logs or process arguments; keep online-mode authentication distinct from offline identity.
 4. **Adapt gameplay input and Android lifecycle behavior.** Reuse and adapt Pojav touch-control concepts for Horizon’s input model: movement/look, break/place/use, jump/sneak/sprint, hotbar, inventory, pause, keyboard, and gamepad where supported. Handle focus changes, rotation/resizing, pause/resume, and clean game shutdown.
 5. **Validate and document the MVP.** Build a debug APK for the supported ABI, run available Rust/Android tests, and smoke-test sign-in, standalone offline play, controls, suspend/resume, and exit on a device or emulator. Document build/setup requirements, license notices, and known platform limits.
 
 ## Considerations
 
 - The existing Rust launcher uses desktop GPUI, OS keychains, and process launching; it is not itself an Android UI/runtime. Horizon’s game is native Rust, so Pojav’s JVM, LWJGL shim, and Java-game launcher path are not the integration target.
 - The Rust client has desktop-oriented input and window/platform code. Android support may require conditional dependencies and an Android-specific event/surface lifecycle, not only a Gradle wrapper.
 - Microsoft sign-in depends on a valid app registration and the Minecraft services. The Android flow must retain explicit failures for unavailable configuration, network, or ownership/profile validation; standalone offline play remains separate.
 - PojavLauncher’s root license is LGPL-3.0. Audit source files and bundled dependencies individually before reuse and preserve required notices/source obligations.
 - A complete feature-for-feature port of Horizon’s desktop launcher is outside this MVP. The first release is scoped to the working gameplay path and account/input behaviors above.
 - The checkout already reports 3,414 tracked files deleted at its root, while `horizon/` and `PojavLauncher/` appear as untracked trees. Do not restore, delete, or otherwise alter those root changes as part of this work.

## [§](#android)Android

The Android backend builds on (and exposes types from) the [`ndk`](https://docs.rs/ndk/) crate.

Native Android applications need some form of “glue” crate that is responsible for defining the main entry point for your Rust application as well as tracking various life-cycle events and synchronizing with the main JVM thread.

Winit uses the [android-activity](https://docs.rs/android-activity/) as a glue crate (prior to `0.28` it used [ndk-glue](https://github.com/rust-windowing/android-ndk-rs/tree/master/ndk-glue)).

The version of the glue crate that your application depends on _must_ match the version that Winit depends on because the glue crate is responsible for your application’s main entry point. If Cargo resolves multiple versions, they will clash.

`winit` glue compatibility table:

| winit | ndk-glue                   |
| ----- | -------------------------- |
| 0.30  | `android-activity = "0.6"` |
| 0.29  | `android-activity = "0.5"` |
| 0.28  | `android-activity = "0.4"` |
| 0.27  | `ndk-glue = "0.7"`         |
| 0.26  | `ndk-glue = "0.5"`         |
| 0.25  | `ndk-glue = "0.3"`         |
| 0.24  | `ndk-glue = "0.2"`         |

The recommended way to avoid a conflict with the glue version is to avoid explicitly depending on the `android-activity` crate, and instead consume the API that is re-exported by Winit under `winit::platform::android::activity::*`

Running on an Android device needs a dynamic system library. Add this to Cargo.toml:

```toml
[lib]
name = "main"
crate-type = ["cdylib"]
```

All Android applications are based on an `Activity` subclass, and the `android-activity` crate is designed to support different choices for this base class. Your application _must_ specify the base class it needs via a feature flag:

| Base Class                                                               | Feature Flag              | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NativeActivity`                                                         | `android-native-activity` | Built-in to Android - it is possible to use without compiling any Java or Kotlin code. Java or Kotlin code may be needed to subclass `NativeActivity` to access some platform features. It does not derive from the [`AndroidAppCompat`](https://developer.android.com/reference/androidx/appcompat/app/AppCompatActivity) base class.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| [`GameActivity`](https://developer.android.com/games/agdk/game-activity) | `android-game-activity`   | Derives from [`AndroidAppCompat`](https://developer.android.com/reference/androidx/appcompat/app/AppCompatActivity), a defacto standard `Activity` base class that helps support a wider range of Android versions. Requires a build system that can compile Java or Kotlin and fetch Android dependencies from a [Maven repository](https://developer.android.com/jetpack/androidx/releases/games) (or link with an embedded [release](https://developer.android.com/games/agdk/download#agdk-libraries) of [`GameActivity`](https://developer.android.com/games/agdk/game-activity)) |

For more details, refer to these `android-activity` [example applications](https://github.com/rust-mobile/android-activity/tree/main/examples).

### [§](#converting-from-ndk-glue-to-android-activity)Converting from `ndk-glue` to `android-activity`

If your application is currently based on `NativeActivity` via the `ndk-glue` crate and building with `cargo apk`, then the minimal changes would be:

1.  Remove `ndk-glue` from your `Cargo.toml`
2.  Enable the `"android-native-activity"` feature for Winit: `winit = { version = "0.30.13", features = [ "android-native-activity" ] }`
3.  Add an `android_main` entrypoint (as above), instead of using the ’`[ndk_glue::main]` proc macro from `ndk-macros` (optionally add a dependency on `android_logger` and initialize logging as above).
4.  Pass a clone of the `AndroidApp` that your application receives to Winit when building your event loop (as shown above).

Contents of https://docs.rs/android-activity/0.6.0/android_activity/:
# Crate android\_activity 

[Source](../src/android_activity/lib.rs.html#1-869) 

Expand description

A glue layer for building standalone, Rust applications on Android

This crate provides a “glue” layer for building native Rust applications on Android, supporting multiple [`Activity`](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/app/Activity) base classes. It’s comparable to [`android_native_app_glue.c`](https://developer.android.com/ndk/guides/concepts#naa) for C/C++ applications.

Currently the crate supports two `Activity` base classes:

1.  [`NativeActivity`](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/app/NativeActivity) - Built in to Android, this doesn’t require compiling any Java or Kotlin code.
2.  [`GameActivity`](https://developer.android.com/games/agdk/integrate-game-activity) - From the Android Game Development Kit, it has more sophisticated input handling support than `NativeActivity`. `GameActivity` is also based on the `AndroidAppCompat` class which can help with supporting a wider range of devices.

Standalone applications based on this crate need to be built as `cdylib` libraries, like:

```
[lib]
crate_type=["cdylib"]
```

and implement a `#[no_mangle]` `android_main` entry point like this:

```
#[no_mangle]
fn android_main(app: AndroidApp) {

}
```

Once your application’s `Activity` class has loaded and it calls `onCreate` then `android-activity` will spawn a dedicated thread to run your `android_main` function, separate from the Java thread that created the corresponding `Activity`.

[`AndroidApp`](struct.AndroidApp.html "struct android_activity::AndroidApp") provides an interface to query state for the application as well as monitor events, such as lifecycle and input events, that are marshalled between the Java thread that owns the `Activity` and the native thread that runs the `android_main()` code.

## [§](#cheaply-clonable-androidapp)Cheaply Clonable [`AndroidApp`](struct.AndroidApp.html "struct android_activity::AndroidApp")

[`AndroidApp`](struct.AndroidApp.html "struct android_activity::AndroidApp") is intended to be something that can be cheaply passed around by referenced within an application. It is reference counted and can be cheaply cloned.

## [§](#send-and-sync-androidapp)`Send` and `Sync` [`AndroidApp`](struct.AndroidApp.html "struct android_activity::AndroidApp")

Although an [`AndroidApp`](struct.AndroidApp.html "struct android_activity::AndroidApp") implements `Send` and `Sync` you do need to take into consideration that some APIs, such as [`AndroidApp::poll_events()`](struct.AndroidApp.html#method.poll_events "method android_activity::AndroidApp::poll_events") are explicitly documented to only be usable from your `android_main()` thread.

## [§](#main-thread-initialization)Main Thread Initialization

Before `android_main()` is called, the following application state is also initialized:

1.  An I/O thread is spawned that will handle redirecting standard input and output to the Android log, visible via `logcat`.
2.  A `JavaVM` and `Activity` instance will be associated with the [`ndk_context`](https://docs.rs/ndk-context/0.1.1/aarch64-linux-android/ndk_context/index.html "mod ndk_context") crate so that other, independent, Rust crates are able to find a JavaVM for making JNI calls.
3.  The `JavaVM` will be attached to the native thread
4.  A [Looper](https://developer.android.com/reference/android/os/Looper) is attached to the Rust native thread.

These are undone after `android_main()` returns

## [§](#android-extensible-enums)Android Extensible Enums

There are numerous enums in the `android-activity` API which are effectively bindings to enums declared in the Android SDK which need to be considered _runtime_ extensible.

Any enum variants that come from the Android SDK may be extended in future versions of Android and your code could be exposed to new variants if you build an application that might be installed on new versions of Android.

This crate follows a convention of adding a hidden `__Unknown(u32)` variant to these enum to ensure we can always do lossless conversions between the integers from the SDK and our corresponding Rust enums. This can be important in case you need to pass certain variants back to the SDK regardless of whether you knew about that variants specific semantics at compile time.

You should never include this `__Unknown(u32)` variant within any exhaustive pattern match and should instead treat the enums like `#[non_exhaustive]` enums that require you to add a catch-all for any `unknown => {}` values.

Any code that would exhaustively include the `__Unknown(u32)` variant when pattern matching can not be guaranteed to be forwards compatible with new releases of `android-activity` which may add new Rust variants to these enums without requiring a breaking semver bump.

You can (infallibly) convert these enums to and from primitive `u32` values using `.into()`:

For example, here is how you could ensure forwards compatibility with both compile-time and runtime extensions of a `SomeEnum` enum:

```
match some_enum {
    SomeEnum::Foo => {},
    SomeEnum::Bar => {},
    unhandled => {
        let sdk_val: u32 = unhandled.into();
        println!("Unhandled enum variant {some_enum:?} has SDK value: {sdk_val}");
    }
}
```

Available on **`android_platform`** only.

Expand description

## [§](#android)Android

The Android backend builds on (and exposes types from) the [`ndk`](https://docs.rs/ndk/) crate.

Native Android applications need some form of “glue” crate that is responsible for defining the main entry point for your Rust application as well as tracking various life-cycle events and synchronizing with the main JVM thread.

Winit uses the [android-activity](https://docs.rs/android-activity/) as a glue crate (prior to `0.28` it used [ndk-glue](https://github.com/rust-windowing/android-ndk-rs/tree/master/ndk-glue)).

The version of the glue crate that your application depends on _must_ match the version that Winit depends on because the glue crate is responsible for your application’s main entry point. If Cargo resolves multiple versions, they will clash.

`winit` glue compatibility table:

| winit | ndk-glue                   |
| ----- | -------------------------- |
| 0.30  | `android-activity = "0.6"` |
| 0.29  | `android-activity = "0.5"` |
| 0.28  | `android-activity = "0.4"` |
| 0.27  | `ndk-glue = "0.7"`         |
| 0.26  | `ndk-glue = "0.5"`         |
| 0.25  | `ndk-glue = "0.3"`         |
| 0.24  | `ndk-glue = "0.2"`         |

The recommended way to avoid a conflict with the glue version is to avoid explicitly depending on the `android-activity` crate, and instead consume the API that is re-exported by Winit under `winit::platform::android::activity::*`

Running on an Android device needs a dynamic system library. Add this to Cargo.toml:

```toml
[lib]
name = "main"
crate-type = ["cdylib"]
```

All Android applications are based on an `Activity` subclass, and the `android-activity` crate is designed to support different choices for this base class. Your application _must_ specify the base class it needs via a feature flag:

| Base Class                                                               | Feature Flag              | Notes                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NativeActivity`                                                         | `android-native-activity` | Built-in to Android - it is possible to use without compiling any Java or Kotlin code. Java or Kotlin code may be needed to subclass `NativeActivity` to access some platform features. It does not derive from the [`AndroidAppCompat`](https://developer.android.com/reference/androidx/appcompat/app/AppCompatActivity) base class.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| [`GameActivity`](https://developer.android.com/games/agdk/game-activity) | `android-game-activity`   | Derives from [`AndroidAppCompat`](https://developer.android.com/reference/androidx/appcompat/app/AppCompatActivity), a defacto standard `Activity` base class that helps support a wider range of Android versions. Requires a build system that can compile Java or Kotlin and fetch Android dependencies from a [Maven repository](https://developer.android.com/jetpack/androidx/releases/games) (or link with an embedded [release](https://developer.android.com/games/agdk/download#agdk-libraries) of [`GameActivity`](https://developer.android.com/games/agdk/game-activity)) |

For more details, refer to these `android-activity` [example applications](https://github.com/rust-mobile/android-activity/tree/main/examples).

### [§](#converting-from-ndk-glue-to-android-activity)Converting from `ndk-glue` to `android-activity`

If your application is currently based on `NativeActivity` via the `ndk-glue` crate and building with `cargo apk`, then the minimal changes would be:

1.  Remove `ndk-glue` from your `Cargo.toml`
2.  Enable the `"android-native-activity"` feature for Winit: `winit = { version = "0.30.13", features = [ "android-native-activity" ] }`
3.  Add an `android_main` entrypoint (as above), instead of using the ’`[ndk_glue::main]` proc macro from `ndk-macros` (optionally add a dependency on `android_logger` and initialize logging as above).
4.  Pass a clone of the `AndroidApp` that your application receives to Winit when building your event loop (as shown above).

## [§](#pollster)Pollster

Pollster is an incredibly minimal async executor for Rust that lets you block a thread until a future completes.

[![Cargo](https://img.shields.io/crates/v/pollster.svg)](https://crates.io/crates/pollster) [![Documentation](https://docs.rs/pollster/badge.svg)](https://docs.rs/pollster) [![License](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT%2FApache--2.0-blue.svg)](https://github.com/zesterer/pollster) ![actions-badge](https://github.com/zesterer/pollster/workflows/Rust/badge.svg?branch=master)

```
use pollster::FutureExt as _;

let my_fut = async {};

let result = my_fut.block_on();
```

That’s it. That’s all it does. Nothing more, nothing less. No need to pull in 50 crates to evaluate a future.

### [§](#why-is-this-useful)Why is this useful?

Now that `async` functions are stable, we’re increasingly seeing libraries all over the Rust ecosystem expose `async` APIs. This is great for those wanting to build highly concurrent web applications!

However, many of us are _not_ building highly concurrent web applications, but end up faced with an `async` function that we can’t easily call from synchronous code. If you’re in this position, then `pollster` is for you: it allows you to evaluate a future in-place without spinning up a heavyweight runtime like `tokio` or `async_std`.

### [§](#minimalism)Minimalism

Pollster is built with the [UNIX ethos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_philosophy#Do_One_Thing_and_Do_It_Well) in mind: do one thing, and do it well. It has no dependencies, compiles quickly, and is composed of only ~100 lines of well-audited code.

### [§](#behaviour)Behaviour

Pollster will synchronously block the thread until a future completes. It will not spin: instead, it will place the thread into a waiting state until the future has been polled to completion.

parts.text:
Integrate the proven Android Vulkan rendering path into the correct Horizon project and deliver the first working, buildable milestone.

## Verified starting point
An isolated Rust rendering probe exists at:

`/workspaces/android-render-probe`

It successfully builds into an Android APK. I installed it on a physical Xiaomi Redmi Note 13 running Android 15.

Confirmed log evidence:

`PRESENTED_FRAME count=1 backend=Vulkan adapter=Adreno (TM) 610 width=2400 height=1080 format=Rgba8UnormSrgb`

The probe uses Rust, winit 0.30.13, wgpu 30.0.1 and Vulkan. It displays a full-screen pink test frame. This proves that a Vulkan frame can be presented on the physical device; it does NOT prove Horizon integration is complete.

The repository is `/workspaces/horizon-android`. Its root contains `horizon` and `PojavLauncher`.

## Main objective
Investigate the existing architecture, identify the correct integration target, implement the smallest technically sound integration, build it, and prepare an APK that I can install and test on my physical phone.

Do not assume that the probe should replace the existing renderer. Determine how the existing project works first.

## Execution plan

1. **Establish the baseline.** Inspect the repository instructions, Git status, existing changes, project structure, Android entry points, build system, rendering architecture and native code. Record the initial Git status outside the repository so you can verify that pre-existing changes remain preserved.
2. **Choose the correct target.** Inspect both `horizon` and `PojavLauncher`. Determine which application actually needs the Android rendering integration and whether winit/wgpu can fit its existing lifecycle and rendering architecture. Do not modify PojavLauncher just because it exists in the repository.
3. **Implement a minimal vertical slice.** Reuse the isolated probe as a technical reference. Make only the changes needed to integrate the rendering path into the correct target. Preserve existing functionality and avoid an unnecessary rewrite. Keep the probe available as a known-working reference.
4. **Build and verify.** Run the relevant checks and build the Android debug APK. Diagnose and fix errors caused by your own changes. Verify that the APK contains the required native ARM64 libraries and has the correct Android entry point and manifest configuration.
5. **Prepare physical-device testing.** Provide the exact APK path, installation command for Windows PowerShell, launch instructions and focused `adb logcat` command. Distinguish successful compilation from successful rendering on the physical phone. Do not claim device testing passed until new evidence proves it.
6. **Report the result.** Summarize the architecture discovered, files changed, build/test outcomes, known limitations and the next concrete milestone. If the current architecture makes the proposed integration unsafe or incompatible, explain the specific blocker and implement only a safe, useful intermediate step.

## Critical repository safety rules

- There are substantial pre-existing tracked deletions and untracked files. They are intentional or otherwise outside your authority to discard. Preserve them all.
- Never run `git reset`, `git clean`, `git restore`, destructive checkout commands, or stash operations.
- Do not delete, move, overwrite or recreate existing project files wholesale.
- Inspect existing diffs before editing files that already have local changes. Apply narrow patches and preserve the existing work.
- Do not commit, push, or create a pull request.
- Do not delete or overwrite `/workspaces/horizon-android/app-debug.apk`; it is the already-tested standalone probe APK.
- Do not declare success solely because a build passes. The final goal is a correct integration that can be tested on the actual Android device.
- Do not stop after writing a plan if you can safely continue implementing and testing. Work through the steps autonomously, respecting all constraints above.
Start by inspecting the current state, then proceed toward the smallest working integration.">

# Horizon Horizon is Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3 rewritten in Rust: a native game that reads the same worlds, follows the same rules and generates the same terrain as the Java game, and is checked against it by 281 differential harnesses. You play it through a small launcher, on the files from your own copy of Minecraft. It is free, open source and unofficial. > Not an official Minecraft product. Not approved by or associated with Mojang or Microsoft. Horizon contains no Minecraft code, assets or data: you need your own legally obtained copy of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3. ## Download Horizon is installed through **the Horizon launcher**. Get it from [playhorizon.dev](https://playhorizon.dev) (the Download button picks your system) or from [the launcher releases](https://github.com/horizon-rust/horizon/releases?q=launcher-v&expanded=true), for Linux x86-64, macOS on Apple Silicon or Windows x64. The launcher installs and updates the game, prepares its files from your own copy of Minecraft, and updates itself. **You need** a Microsoft account that owns Minecraft: Java Edition (the launcher signs in with it, as other launchers do; see [Microsoft account](docs/microsoft-account.md)); Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3, played once (the official launcher, Prism, MultiMC and other launchers all work); a Java 25 runtime, for the one-time preparation; and a GPU with Vulkan on Linux and Windows, or any Apple Silicon Mac. Step by step, with macOS's first-open prompt and the first launch: [Install and first launch](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/install).
## What works today The [documentation](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/) covers each of these. - **The game:** singleplayer with vanilla's world generation, mobs, villagers, raids, redstone, every command, the HUD and the recipe book, on saves in vanilla's format. Worlds from 1.8 to 26.2 are upgraded as vanilla does. [Status table](#project-status). - **Horizon's own extras:** new menus (vanilla's are one setting away), graphics presets, distant terrain up to 1024 chunks, controller support, optional zoom, minimap and more, all off by default where they would change the vanilla look. See [Settings](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/settings). - **Resource packs and data packs:** resource packs work, and data packs load functions, predicates and item modifiers. - **Playing with others:** invite friends from the pause menu's Friends button with a code, Open to LAN, and joining servers, online-mode ones with the Microsoft account the launcher signs in with. See [Multiplayer](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/multiplayer). - **Mods:** Horizon has its own mod system (Rust compiled to WebAssembly). Java mod jars do not run. See [Mods and data packs](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/mods). Screenshots, captured in the Rust client itself with vanilla assets and no mods or shaders:
## Host a server The launcher's **Servers** page creates, starts, backs up and updates a Horizon server with buttons, and invites friends over Tailscale. On a VPS, `horizon-server` installs with one command and runs without Java. Guide: [Host a server](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/hosting) ([reference](docs/hosting.md)). ## Modpacks The launcher's **Modpacks** page imports a Modrinth or CurseForge pack, shows which of its mods Horizon can carry over, and plays the ones it can as their own profile. Today that means content mods made of data and assets; mods with Java code are not ported yet. See [Modpacks](https://playhorizon.dev/docs/modpacks). ## Agent control AI agents and scripts can play Horizon. `horizon-ctl`, shipped beside the game in every release folder, is a command line that reads the game as JSON and acts like a player; `horizon-ctl mcp` serves the same commands as an MCP server (one tool per command, screenshots returned as images). ```sh horizon-ctl launch --world Survival --seed 5 --wait # finds the version the launcher installed horizon-ctl state # position, health, food, target, screen... horizon-ctl find-block birch_log # the nearest logs horizon-ctl goto -0.5 65 -2.5 --near 2.5 # walks there along a path horizon-ctl break -1 65 -3 # mines it; replies with the drops horizon-ctl open-inventory && horizon-ctl click-slot 0 # menus: slots, buttons by label, text fields ``` Commands block until the action is done and reply with what happened; errors are JSON with distinct exit codes, `horizon-ctl help` lists every command and `horizon-ctl COMMAND --help` explains one with examples. It talks to the game over a Unix socket on Linux and macOS and over a token-protected localhost port on Windows. See [Agent control in the native client guide](docs/native-client.md#agent-control-horizon-ctl-and-mcp). ## Build from source For developers. Requirements: Rust 1.90 or newer, Python 3.10 or newer, JDK 25, and on Linux the ALSA and udev development headers (`libasound2-dev libudev-dev` on Debian and Ubuntu). Development and the vanilla harnesses run on Linux. Horizon contains no game files and never downloads them. It builds its resources from **your own copy** of Minecraft: Java Edition 26.3, verified against the checksums in `research-lock.json`: 1. **Client:** install Java Edition with the official launcher and play 26.3 once. Horizon reads `versions/26.3/`, `libraries/` and `assets/` from the launcher's game directory (`~/.minecraft` on Linux). If yours lives elsewhere, pass `--minecraft-dir` or set `HORIZON_MINECRAFT_DIR`. 2. **Server jar:** the 26.3 server jar, from the `downloads.server.url` in your launcher's `versions/26.3/26.3.json` (or [minecraft.net/download/server](https:/

 ```sh
 cargo run --release -p horizon-client
 ```
 
 The launcher is its own Cargo workspace in `launcher/` (`cd launcher && cargo run`; on NixOS, `nix-shell` first).
 
 ## Vanilla first
 
 Wherever vanilla has a feature, vanilla is the specification, down to the order of random calls. "Parity" here
 means Horizon gives the same results as the pinned 26.3 client and server for the same inputs, checked by a
 **harness**: a `tools/test_*_parity.py` script that runs a small Java oracle against the real game and a Rust
 probe against Horizon, and compares their outputs. There are about 290 of them.
 
 - **Read the vanilla code before writing Horizon's.** `tools/rea_vanilla.py` queries the pinned game bytecode:
   `python3 tools/rea_vanilla.py method net.minecraft.world.level.block.DispenserBlock dispenseFrom`.
   Say in your pull request which vanilla classes and methods you followed.
 - **Gameplay changes come with a harness**, new or extended, so the next change can't silently break them.
   [The parity workflow](docs/parity-workflow.md) shows how harnesses run; copy a nearby one.
 - **Horizon's own features** (the launcher, the new menus) follow [the design system](docs/design-system.md) and are
   off by default wherever they would change the vanilla look.
 - **Everything players run is Rust.** Python and Java are fine for dev tools and harness drivers in `tools/`, never
   for player-facing code.
 
 Never commit game files, decompiled source or prepared resources (`.local/`): `tools/check_public_tree.py` rejects
 them (`git config core.hooksPath .githooks` runs it before every commit).
 The pre-push hook checks the full history reachable from the branches and tags being pushed. Run
 `python3 tools/check_public_tree.py --history` to audit the history of all local refs.
 
 ## Only original code
 
 Horizon's code is written from Minecraft 26.3 itself and from public documentation, never from another mod, loader
 or renderer. Don't read, copy, translate or paraphrase the source of Iris, OptiFine, Sodium or any other project,
 and don't send code an AI tool wrote from it. Their user documentation and file formats are fine to read, and their
 packs and mods are fine to run and observe. Shader packs were removed on 24 October 2026 (#1561) because their code
 had been written from another project's source; they come back only as a clean-room rewrite from a written
 description of the pack format.
 
 ## Before asking for review
 
 Run the self-check and paste the block it prints into your pull request:
 
 ```sh
 python3 tools/pr_ready.py --base upstream/main   # or origin/main if you work on the main repository
 ```
 
 It looks at what your branch changes and runs what matters: rustfmt, clippy with warnings denied, the tests of the
 crates you touched (and the launcher's), generated files, `Cargo.lock`, the Python tests, and the vanilla harnesses
 your change can affect. Without the vanilla data on your machine it lists those harnesses instead; CI runs them.
 `--quick` skips the harnesses. It exits non-zero when something fails.
 
 For the game workspace, Clippy checks all targets of the touched crates and their transitive workspace dependents,
 including examples. The dependency scope includes optional, platform, build and development dependencies.
 Tests run library, binary, integration and doc tests without building unrelated example executables. Shared Cargo
 configuration and toolchain changes select the whole workspace; CI also keeps its workspace-wide checks.
 
 ## Pull requests
 
 - **Small.** One change per pull request, under about 500 lines of code where you can; split bigger work into
   pieces that each make sense alone. Small pull requests get reviewed and merged the same day.
 - **Fill in the template**: what and why, the vanilla reference, the pr_ready block, screenshots for anything you
   can see.
 - **Tick "Allow edits by maintainers".** When something small is left (a lint, a rebase, a nit) we push the fixup
   ourselves instead of sending it back to you; only design questions come back.
 - **Labels** (we set them if you can't): `feature` when players get something new (it appears under "New" in the
   release notes), `skip-release` when players see no change (tooling, docs, tests), nothing for a fix.
   `release-now` is for crash fixes that shouldn't wait. pr_ready suggests one.
 
 Who reviews and merges: the Horizon Team, on CI for ordinary pull requests; risky ones (saves, network, world
 generation, the launcher's updates) wait for a local proof first ([merging](docs/release-flow.md#merging)).
 
 Every merge to main is released automatically ([release flow](docs/release-flow.md)), so main always stays playable.
 How agents, checks, releases and signed updates keep this safe: [security](docs/security.md).
 
 ## Parity checks on forks
 
 The `verify` check (formatting, lints, tests) runs on every pull request. The `parity` check runs the affected
 harnesses on a maintainer's machine, which holds the game files, so it never runs a fork's code on its own: a
 maintainer reads your change, then adds the `run-parity` label, which runs it once on your current commit. After
 new pushes, we add it again.
 
 ## Talk to us
 
 [Discord](https://discord.gg/HcTeMZxe5E) for questions and ideas, [issues](https://github.com/horizon-rust/horizon/issues)
 for bugs. If you want to take something on, say so in its issue so nobody else starts the same work.

**Exploring Android compatibility issues**

I see there's a problem with compiling the horizon-client for Android due to the arboard library not being supported. It looks like we might need to implement some sort of feature gating or create a stub for Android. The app shouldn’t require the entire horizon-client library. If we could make arboard specific to targets or adjust configuration in `control.rs`, it might help. I need to inspect how arboard is utilized in the client library. I'll search for its usage in `clipboard.rs` and evaluate the architecture.

**Analyzing Cargo dependencies for Android**

I'm checking the `client Cargo.toml` dependencies to see if arboard is a direct dependency by running `cargo tree -i arboard --target android`. I don't see arboard listed in the horizon-client dependencies, so I need to search more thoroughly. I'll need to check `horizon-client-core` too since this project runs on Linux. Compiling the full client for Android might introduce additional incompatibilities. The user is primarily concerned with the rendering milestone, so perhaps I should separate the render check module from the horizon-client dependency. Moving it to a new crate could be a safe step.

**Implementing Android-specific rendering**

The implementation plan mentions creating an "Android-only native render-check entry point" using existing winit and wgpu versions, but it's not specifically part of the horizon-client. Instead, we'll anticipate an Android-only Rust module with a NativeActivity cdylib entry-point crate within Horizon. I can find this in `android/native/src/lib.rs`, allowing us to use winit and wgpu directly without depending on horizon-client. This keeps it under the `horizon/android/native` project while ensuring version matching for proper packaging.

**Evaluating Horizon project integration**

It seems the new app project under Horizon is fine, but it doesn’t link to the game runtime. I think we could set shared dependencies from the Horizon manifest. I want to focus on fixing the arboard portability first, perhaps as a second task. The architecture has a blocker because arboard doesn’t support Android—but we can make the probe self-contained without needing the entire client. I'm curious if we can build the Android app as its own target within the workspace.

**Considering integration options**

The user first asked about achieving the smallest technically sound integration, and we've decided to start with an initial smoke test. I think we can create a new debug diagnostic pipeline within the Horizon project while keeping the runtime untouched. I must mention an architecture blocker and plan the next step. For the full horizon-client import, I wonder if we could patch arboard. The user wants to build the actual APK, so I’ll focus on Android support, potentially fixing specific missing implementations.

**Identifying integration blockers**

It looks like the initial failure is with arboard. I think we could use `#[cfg(not(target_os="android"))]` for the clipboard and stub that out. But there might be more failures ahead since this is an actual integration blocker that needs some adaptations. The user's plan specifies that if the current architecture creates safety issues, I should explain the specific blockers and focus on safe, useful solutions. I see that the full client doesn’t build for Android due to arboard, so we should keep the render-check app separate for now.

**Revising project structure**

I need to re-edit by removing the patch module and adding render.rs. I think applying the patch should be done manually, as it might be easier to move the file from the old location to the new one. I'll update the module after that. However, I need to keep in mind that the `android.rs` module code is currently in the client crate, so I'll have to move it to native/src/render.rs. That's important!

The first Android-target check exposed a specific client portability blocker: the existing Horizon library depends on `arboard`, which currently has no Android clipboard backend. Rather than silently changing clipboard behavior or expanding this render milestone into a client port, I’m isolating the asset-free smoke APK in Horizon’s Android workspace, using the same pinned winit/wgpu stack. The actual Horizon game renderer remains unmodified; this is explicitly a rendering-validation shell, not gameplay.

 # Horizon Android Vulkan render check
 
 This is the first Android build milestone for Horizon: a small ARM64 NativeActivity APK that drives winit 0.30.13 and wgpu 30.0.1 through Android's Vulkan surface lifecycle and presents a visible diagnostic frame.
 
 **This is not the Horizon game client.** The smoke APK does not load a world, use the existing `horizon-client::gfx::Renderer`, or bundle Minecraft files. It leaves the desktop renderer and PojavLauncher unchanged. No Minecraft resources are needed for this test.
 
 ## Architecture
 
 - Android starts `android.app.NativeActivity` from `app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`; its library name is `horizon_android`.
 - `android/native` builds `libhorizon_android.so` as a Rust `cdylib`. `android_main(AndroidApp)` initializes Android logging and starts the render check.
 - winit receives the `AndroidApp` through `EventLoopBuilderExtAndroid::with_android_app`. Its resumed/suspended/window events create and release the probe surface/renderer.
 - wgpu is restricted to Vulkan for this diagnostic. The app logs the adapter, driver, surface format/size, lifecycle, and `PRESENTED_FRAME` after the queue submits and presents a frame.
 - The diagnostic uses the same pinned winit and wgpu versions as Horizon. It is intentionally separate from `horizon-client::gfx::Renderer`.
 
 ## Build the debug APK on Linux x86-64
 
 Toolchain baseline: Rust 1.95.0, JDK 17, Gradle 8.13, Android Gradle Plugin 8.7.2, SDK Platform/Build Tools 35, and NDK 27.2.12479018. Rust 1.95.0 is required by the current Horizon workspace (`horizon-mods`); it is newer than the standalone probe's original Rust baseline.
 
 Install the Android Rust target once:
 
 ```sh
 rustup toolchain install 1.95.0 --profile minimal
 rustup target add aarch64-linux-android --toolchain 1.95.0
 ```
 
 Set the Android/JDK environment and build:
 
 ```sh
 export JAVA_HOME="$HOME/.local/jdks/temurin-17.0.13+11"
 export ANDROID_HOME="$HOME/Android/Sdk"
 export ANDROID_SDK_ROOT="$ANDROID_HOME"
 export ANDROID_NDK_HOME="$ANDROID_HOME/ndk/27.2.12479018"
 export ANDROID_NDK_ROOT="$ANDROID_NDK_HOME"
 export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools:$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH"
 
 cd horizon/android
 ./gradlew --no-daemon --stacktrace :app:assembleDebug
 ```
 
 Gradle runs the pinned Rust toolchain for `aarch64-linux-android`, uses the NDK's API-26 linker, and copies the shared library into generated build output before packaging. The APK is:
 
 ```text
 horizon/android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
 ```
 
 ## Install and test on a physical Android device (Windows PowerShell)
 
 Use an arm64 device with Android API 26+ and Vulkan 1.0 support. From the repository root, install and launch:
 
 ```powershell
 $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
 $apk = (Resolve-Path .\horizon\android\app\build\outputs\apk\debug\app-debug.apk).Path
 adb devices -l
 adb install -r $apk
 adb shell am force-stop dev.playhorizon.horizon
 adb logcat -c
 adb shell am start -n dev.playhorizon.horizon/android.app.NativeActivity
 Start-Sleep -Seconds 10
 adb logcat -d -v threadtime -s HorizonAndroid:I HorizonAndroid:E AndroidRuntime:E |
     Tee-Object -FilePath .\horizon-android-render.log
 adb shell screencap -p /sdcard/horizon-android-render.png
 adb pull /sdcard/horizon-android-render.png .\horizon-android-render.png
 ```
 
 A successful device render must show the non-black diagnostic frame and matching `PRESENTED_FRAME` evidence identifying the Vulkan backend, adapter, dimensions, and format. The APK build and a successful Activity launch alone do not prove presentation. Preserve the device model/API/ABI, GPU/driver, full relevant log, and screenshot or video when reporting the result.
 
 The APK output above is separate from `/workspaces/horizon-android/app-debug.apk`, the already-tested standalone probe APK; this build does not overwrite that file.
 
 ## Known blockers and next milestone
 
 - The existing `horizon-client` crate is not currently an Android build target. An Android-target check while testing direct linkage failed in `arboard 3.6.1`: that dependency selects no clipboard implementation for Android. Do not paper over this by silently disabling clipboard behavior. A deliberate Android clipboard backend or a scoped platform abstraction is needed before wiring the full client.
 - The smoke APK does not import Minecraft resources or enter a world. A later client milestone must define a user-owned resource import into app-private storage, adapt filesystem/audio/input assumptions, then validate the real game renderer and local-world entry on hardware.
 - Physical-device testing of this Horizon APK is still outstanding. The separate standalone probe's successful Xiaomi Redmi Note 13 run does not count as evidence for this APK.

I’m thinking about whether `cargo fmt --all` will affect preexisting files, even if they weren't formatted before — it could. Checking `git status` shows only the root but untracked files may hide under `horizon`. Running `cargo fmt` modifies Rust files potentially, so I might want to compare file hashes. It's important to stick to the constraint of not modifying unrelated changes. I wonder if inspecting mtimes could help me here since `cargo fmt` writes only if necessary, possibly impacting thousands of files.

**Evaluating project file changes**

The user mentioned not to overwrite project files wholesale, but we ran a workspace-wide formatter, which might not be ideal. Now I need to identify what changed using `git`, but the root status shows all untracked files with no diffs. Since Horizon doesn't have a `.git` directory, I can't compare to HEAD. I could check the recent modification times to see how many files were touched. I wonder if `cargo fmt` rewrites unchanged Rust sources, but likely it won't if the output is the same.

**Checking build artifacts and updates**

I'm thinking about how to inspect mtime files using `find horizon -type f -mmin`, but cargo build generates many artifacts, including Cargo.lock. Source file mtime might help, yet it's not really necessary if the formatting is a no-op after the first run since cargo fmt check passed. The user wants to keep all pre-existing modifications, so running rustfmt on our files instead of the whole workspace might be a good plan. Cargo update unexpectedly modified Cargo.lock, adding a package and android dependency. I should check the APK manifest and symbols next.

**Testing adb and checking configurations**

I need to test `adb devices -l` to confirm that no devices are connected because the command directly points to the Android SDK path. The current PATH doesn’t include it, but I can execute the command with the absolute path. Last time, `command -v adb` returned blank, which might indicate that platform-tools aren't installed. I’ll try running `"$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools/adb" devices -l`, which should show no devices. I'll also be looking into the errors with `arboard 3.6.1` and checking for the required symbols like `android_main`.

**Reviewing android_main functionality**

I’ve confirmed that the probe was successful, and it seems the winit Android documentation indicates the signature uses `pub fn android_main(app: AndroidApp)`. In older versions, it was `#[no_mangle] pub fn android_main(app: AndroidApp)`, which looks correct. I need to improve error handling since `android_main` currently logs errors but then returns, allowing the event loop to exit. It's important not to have silent failures.  # Horizon Android Vulkan render check
 
 This is the first Android build milestone for Horizon: a small ARM64 NativeActivity APK that drives winit 0.30.13 and wgpu 30.0.1 through Android's Vulkan surface lifecycle and presents a visible diagnostic frame.
 
 **This is not the Horizon game client.** The smoke APK does not load a world, use the existing `horizon-client::gfx::Renderer`, or bundle Minecraft files. It leaves the desktop renderer and PojavLauncher unchanged. No Minecraft resources are needed for this test.
 
 ## Architecture
 
 - Android starts `android.app.NativeActivity` from `app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`; its library name is `horizon_android`.
 - `android/native` builds `libhorizon_android.so` as a Rust `cdylib`. `android_main(AndroidApp)` initializes Android logging and starts the render check.
 - winit receives the `AndroidApp` through `EventLoopBuilderExtAndroid::with_android_app`. Its resumed/suspended/window events create and release the probe surface/renderer.
 - wgpu is restricted to Vulkan for this diagnostic. The app logs the adapter, driver, surface format/size, lifecycle, and `PRESENTED_FRAME` after the queue submits and presents a frame.
 - The diagnostic uses the same pinned winit and wgpu versions as Horizon. It is intentionally separate from `horizon-client::gfx::Renderer`.
 
 ## Build the debug APK on Linux x86-64
 
 Toolchain baseline: Rust 1.95.0, JDK 17, Gradle 8.13, Android Gradle Plugin 8.7.2, SDK Platform/Build Tools 35, and NDK 27.2.12479018. Rust 1.95.0 is required by the current Horizon workspace (`horizon-mods`); it is newer than the standalone probe's original Rust baseline.
 
 Install the Android Rust target once:
 
 ```sh
 rustup toolchain install 1.95.0 --profile minimal
 rustup target add aarch64-linux-android --toolchain 1.95.0
 ```
 
 Set the Android/JDK environment and build:
 
 ```sh
 export JAVA_HOME="$HOME/.local/jdks/temurin-17.0.13+11"
 export ANDROID_HOME="$HOME/Android/Sdk"
 export ANDROID_SDK_ROOT="$ANDROID_HOME"
 export ANDROID_NDK_HOME="$ANDROID_HOME/ndk/27.2.12479018"
 export ANDROID_NDK_ROOT="$ANDROID_NDK_HOME"
 export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$ANDROID_HOME/cmdline-tools/latest/bin:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools:$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH"
 
 sdkmanager --licenses
 sdkmanager --install "platforms;android-35" "build-tools;35.0.0" "ndk;27.2.12479018"
 
 cd horizon/android
 ./gradlew --no-daemon --stacktrace :app:assembleDebug
 ```
 
 Gradle runs the pinned Rust toolchain for `aarch64-linux-android`, uses the NDK's API-26 linker, and copies the shared library into generated build output before packaging. The APK is:
 
 ```text
 horizon/android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
 ```
 
 ## Install and test on a physical Android device (Windows PowerShell)
 
 Use an arm64 device with Android API 26+ and Vulkan 1.0 support. From the repository root, install and launch:
 
 ```powershell
 $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
 $apk = (Resolve-Path .\horizon\android\app\build\outputs\apk\debug\app-debug.apk).Path
 adb devices -l
 adb install -r $apk
 adb shell am force-stop dev.playhorizon.horizon
 adb logcat -c
 adb shell am start -n dev.playhorizon.horizon/android.app.NativeActivity
 Start-Sleep -Seconds 10
 adb logcat -d -v threadtime -s HorizonAndroid:I AndroidRuntime:E |
     Tee-Object -FilePath .\horizon-android-render.log
 @(
     "manufacturer=$(adb shell getprop ro.product.manufacturer)"
     "model=$(adb shell getprop ro.product.model)"
     "android=$(adb shell getprop ro.build.version.release)"
     "api=$(adb shell getprop ro.build.version.sdk)"
     "abi=$(adb shell getprop ro.product.cpu.abi)"
 ) | Tee-Object -FilePath .\horizon-android-device.txt
 adb shell screencap -p /sdcard/horizon-android-render.png
 adb pull /sdcard/horizon-android-render.png .\horizon-android-render.png
 ```
 
 A successful device render must show the non-black diagnostic frame and matching `PRESENTED_FRAME` evidence identifying the Vulkan backend, adapter, dimensions, and format. The APK build and a successful Activity launch alone do not prove presentation. Preserve the device model/API/ABI, GPU/driver, full relevant log, and screenshot or video when reporting the result.
 
 The APK output above is separate from `/workspaces/horizon-android/app-debug.apk`, the already-tested standalone probe APK; this build does not overwrite that file.
 
 ## Known blockers and next milestone
 
 - The existing `horizon-client` crate is not currently an Android build target. An Android-target check while testing direct linkage failed in `arboard 3.6.1`: that dependency selects no clipboard implementation for Android. Do not paper over this by silently disabling clipboard behavior. A deliberate Android clipboard backend or a scoped platform abstraction is needed before wiring the full client.
 - The smoke APK does not import Minecraft resources or enter a world. A later client milestone must define a user-owned resource import into app-private storage, adapt filesystem/audio/input assumptions, then validate the real game renderer and local-world entry on hardware.
 - Physical-device testing of this Horizon APK is still outstanding. The separate standalone probe's successful Xiaomi Redmi Note 13 run does not count as evidence for this APK.

The APK built under `horizon/android/` has been installed and tested on a physical Xiaomi Redmi Note 13 running Android 15.

## Goal
Determine and resolve the Android-specific blockers that prevent the existing Horizon client from building and starting on Android. Progress toward launching the actual client using its existing application architecture and renderer rather than permanently replacing it with the smoke-test app.

1. Inspect the current implementation and existing diffs before changing anything. Identify the real Horizon client entry point, rendering initialization, window/event lifecycle, filesystem assumptions, input/audio dependencies, and Android target configuration.

5. Integrate the existing Horizon client into the Android application lifecycle. Retain the working smoke-test APK and its source as a reference until the actual client path is independently validated.
6. Build an installable ARM64 APK. Verify its manifest, native libraries, and entry point. If it can safely start without Minecraft resources, provide a clear resource-import or missing-resources screen rather than crashing. Do not bundle proprietary Minecraft assets.
7. Test what can be tested in Codespace and provide exact Windows PowerShell commands for physical-device testing. Clearly distinguish build success, successful client startup, successful rendering, and actual gameplay.

- Preserve all pre-existing repository changes, including the known tracked deletions and untracked files.

- Do not overwrite the existing root `app-debug.apk` or the working smoke-test APK.

 # Horizon Android Vulkan render milestone
 
 ## Goal and scope
 
 Add a buildable, asset-free Android debug APK in the correct project, `horizon/`, which initializes Horizon's Android-native winit/wgpu Vulkan surface and presents a visible diagnostic frame on arm64 hardware. Keep this milestone deliberately below gameplay: it must not bundle Minecraft files, require imported assets, alter PojavLauncher, or replace Horizon's existing `gfx::Renderer`. Physical-phone validation of the new APK remains pending until the user runs it and returns evidence.
 
 ## Baseline and architecture
 
 - The root checkout is `/workspaces/horizon-android`; `PojavLauncher/` is a separate, clean nested Git repository and is not the integration target.
 - The Horizon Rust client already depends on winit 0.30.13 and wgpu 30.0.1. Its existing `gfx::Renderer` owns surface creation, device selection, frame rendering, and presentation; Android's current backend order tries Vulkan before GL.
 - There is no Android app project in Horizon and no Android NativeActivity/JNI entry point. The external probe uses winit's `android-native-activity` integration and has already rendered on the user's Xiaomi Redmi Note 13.
 - No Horizon Minecraft resource directory is present. This APK therefore provides a diagnostic launch/render path, not a promise of gameplay; legal user-owned Minecraft data remains outside the APK.
 - Preserve the initial repository state recorded in `baseline-git-status.txt`: 3,414 tracked deletions, 3,416 untracked entries, 0 modified tracked entries, and the recorded porcelain-status SHA-256. Do not clean, restore, or rewrite pre-existing paths.
 
 ## Implementation approach
 
 1. Add an Android-only native render-check entry point within the Horizon project, using the existing winit/wgpu versions and NativeActivity's `android_main(AndroidApp)` lifecycle. Limit the diagnostic to Vulkan and log adapter/driver, surface dimensions/format, lifecycle transitions, and `PRESENTED_FRAME` only after a submitted visible clear frame.
 2. Keep the existing Horizon gameplay renderer and desktop launch behavior unchanged. The diagnostic is only the first APK's smoke-test path; it is not the game renderer and does not claim that Horizon gameplay or Android input/audio is implemented.
 3. Add a small, isolated Gradle Android app under `horizon/android/`, pinned to the same SDK/NDK/AGP/Gradle baseline as the proven probe, with a matching NativeActivity manifest and ARM64 native library. Do not touch the root `app-debug.apk` or the standalone probe.
 4. Build and verify the debug APK; inspect its manifest, NativeActivity library name, and packaged `arm64-v8a` native library. Run Rust formatting and Android-target checks. Record any target/dependency blocker precisely rather than hiding it.
 5. Add concise device-test instructions for Windows PowerShell: APK path, `adb install`, explicit launch, focused logcat capture, and the evidence required to distinguish compilation from successful on-device presentation.
 
 ## Files anticipated
 
 - New Android-only Rust module and NativeActivity `cdylib` entry-point crate under `horizon/`.
 - New Gradle settings/build files, manifest, and wrapper files under `horizon/android/`.
 - A short Android render-check/test guide under `horizon/android/`.
 - Only narrow edits to existing Horizon Cargo metadata if Android target dependencies/features need to be enabled; no edits to PojavLauncher or the existing game renderer.
 
 ## Validation and limitations
 
 - Use Rust 1.90.0, Android NDK 27.2.12479018, SDK Platform/Build Tools 35, AGP 8.7.2, and Gradle 8.13 to reproduce the pinned baseline.
 - Build for `aarch64-linux-android`; verify the resulting APK contains the expected native shared library and launch activity.
 - The standalone probe's physical-device result is evidence for its own APK only. Do not claim the Horizon APK has rendered on-device until new matching logs and a visible screenshot/video are supplied.
 - The first milestone does not implement resource import, launching a local world, touch controls, game audio, authentication, or suspend/resume correctness beyond the minimal surface lifecycle needed by the diagnostic.

 # Horizon Android Vulkan render check
 
 This is the first Android build milestone for Horizon: a small ARM64 NativeActivity APK that drives winit 0.30.13 and wgpu 30.0.1 through Android's Vulkan surface lifecycle and presents a visible diagnostic frame.
 
 **This is not the Horizon game client.** The smoke APK does not load a world, use the existing `horizon-client::gfx::Renderer`, or bundle Minecraft files. It leaves the desktop renderer and PojavLauncher unchanged. No Minecraft resources are needed for this test.
 
 ## Architecture
 
 - Android starts `android.app.NativeActivity` from `app/src/main/AndroidManifest.xml`; its library name is `horizon_android`.
 - `android/native` builds `libhorizon_android.so` as a Rust `cdylib`. `android_main(AndroidApp)` initializes Android logging and starts the render check.
 - winit receives the `AndroidApp` through `EventLoopBuilderExtAndroid::with_android_app`. Its resumed/suspended/window events create and release the probe surface/renderer.
 - wgpu is restricted to Vulkan for this diagnostic. The app logs the adapter, driver, surface format/size, lifecycle, and `PRESENTED_FRAME` after the queue submits and presents a frame.
 - The diagnostic uses the same pinned winit and wgpu versions as Horizon. It is intentionally separate from `horizon-client::gfx::Renderer`.
 
 ## Build the debug APK on Linux x86-64
 
 Toolchain baseline: Rust 1.95.0, JDK 17, Gradle 8.13, Android Gradle Plugin 8.7.2, SDK Platform/Build Tools 35, and NDK 27.2.12479018. Rust 1.95.0 is required by the current Horizon workspace (`horizon-mods`); it is newer than the standalone probe's original Rust baseline.
 
 Install the Android Rust target once:
 
 ```sh
 rustup toolchain install 1.95.0 --profile minimal
 rustup target add aarch64-linux-android --toolchain 1.95.0
 ```
 
 Set the Android/JDK environment and build:
 
 ```sh
 export JAVA_HOME="$HOME/.local/jdks/temurin-17.0.13+11"
 export ANDROID_HOME="$HOME/Android/Sdk"
 export ANDROID_SDK_ROOT="$ANDROID_HOME"
 export ANDROID_NDK_HOME="$ANDROID_HOME/ndk/27.2.12479018"
 export ANDROID_NDK_ROOT="$ANDROID_NDK_HOME"
 export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$ANDROID_HOME/cmdline-tools/latest/bin:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools:$HOME/.cargo/bin:$PATH"
 
 sdkmanager --licenses
 sdkmanager --install "platforms;android-35" "build-tools;35.0.0" "ndk;27.2.12479018"
 
 cd horizon/android
 ./gradlew --no-daemon --stacktrace :app:assembleDebug
 ```
 
 Gradle runs the pinned Rust toolchain for `aarch64-linux-android`, uses the NDK's API-26 linker, and copies the shared library into generated build output before packaging. The APK is:
 
 ```text
 horizon/android/app/build/outputs/apk/debug/app-debug.apk
 ```
 
 ## Install and test on a physical Android device (Windows PowerShell)
 
 Use an arm64 device with Android API 26+ and Vulkan 1.0 support. From the repository root, install and launch:
 
 ```powershell
 $ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
 $apk = (Resolve-Path .\horizon\android\app\build\outputs\apk\debug\app-debug.apk).Path
 adb devices -l
 adb install -r $apk
 adb shell am force-stop dev.playhorizon.horizon
 adb logcat -c
 adb shell am start -n dev.playhorizon.horizon/android.app.NativeActivity
 Start-Sleep -Seconds 10
 adb logcat -d -v threadtime -s HorizonAndroid:I AndroidRuntime:E |
     Tee-Object -FilePath .\horizon-android-render.log
 @(
     "manufacturer=$(adb shell getprop ro.product.manufacturer)"
     "model=$(adb shell getprop ro.product.model)"
     "android=$(adb shell getprop ro.build.version.release)"
     "api=$(adb shell getprop ro.build.version.sdk)"
     "abi=$(adb shell getprop ro.product.cpu.abi)"
 ) | Tee-Object -FilePath .\horizon-android-device.txt
 adb shell screencap -p /sdcard/horizon-android-render.png
 adb pull /sdcard/horizon-android-render.png .\horizon-android-render.png
 ```
 
 A successful device render must show the non-black diagnostic frame and matching `PRESENTED_FRAME` evidence identifying the Vulkan backend, adapter, dimensions, and format. The APK build and a successful Activity launch alone do not prove presentation. Preserve the device model/API/ABI, GPU/driver, full relevant log, and screenshot or video when reporting the result.
 
 The APK output above is separate from `/workspaces/horizon-android/app-debug.apk`, the already-tested standalone probe APK; this build does not overwrite that file.
 
 ## Known blockers and next milestone
 
 - The existing `horizon-client` crate is not currently an Android build target. An Android-target check while testing direct linkage failed in `arboard 3.6.1`: that dependency selects no clipboard implementation for Android. Do not paper over this by silently disabling clipboard behavior. A deliberate Android clipboard backend or a scoped platform abstraction is needed before wiring the full client.
 - The smoke APK does not import Minecraft resources or enter a world. A later client milestone must define a user-owned resource import into app-private storage, adapt filesystem/audio/input assumptions, then validate the real game renderer and local-world entry on hardware.
 - Physical-device testing of this Horizon APK is still outstanding. The separate standalone probe's successful Xiaomi Redmi Note 13 run does not count as evidence for this APK.

 # Horizon native client
 
 `horizon-client` is the playable Rust client for Minecraft Java Edition 26.3.
 It streams a world around the player on worker threads, renders every vanilla
 block model with smooth lighting and biome tints, and runs the validated player
 physics, health and hunger at 20 ticks per second. You can mine with vanilla
 hardness/tool rules, collect drops from the block loot tables, place blocks,
 craft in the 2x2 inventory grid or on a crafting table, and save and reload worlds
 in vanilla's Anvil format.
 
 **Status:** playable; players get it through [the launcher](../launcher/README.md). The [Java parity table](../README.md#project-status)
 in the README scores each subsystem against vanilla and lists what is still
 missing; [Rust rewrite status](rust-parity.md) has the details.
 
 ## Run from a checkout
 
 Use current stable Rust (1.90+) and JDK 25 (Python 3.10+ only for the development
 harnesses). Horizon never
 downloads the game: resource preparation imports **your own copy** (the 26.3
 client from your official launcher install, and the 26.3 server jar you
 downloaded yourself; see [Build from source](../README.md#build-from-source)),
 verifies it against the pinned checksums, runs vanilla's data generator and small
 exporters against those jars, and extracts the jar's assets and data into ignored
 `.local/horizon-client/26.3/`. Sounds (about 380 MB) are copied from your
 launcher's asset store by `horizon-prepare sounds`, each file checked against the asset
 index's SHA-1. Preparation also tries to replace the JAR's gray 1×1 title panorama
 placeholders with the full textures from that asset store. If the store is missing or
 incomplete, preparation logs a warning and keeps the placeholders. To import the panorama
 later without rerunning the Java exporters, run `horizon-prepare panorama` (or
 `cargo run --release -p horizon-prepare -- panorama` in a checkout). Pass
 `--minecraft-dir PATH` when using a different Minecraft installation.
 Prepared resources are private; never commit them.
 
 Preparation is `horizon-prepare` (`crates/horizon-prepare`, Rust): it needs no Python, only
 the JDK, for the small exporters that call Mojang's own code. Release folders ship it beside
 `horizon-client`, and the launcher prepares with it and copies the sounds as part of preparing.
 
 ```sh
 cargo run --release -p horizon-prepare -- --prepare --server-jar ~/Downloads/server.jar
 cargo run --release -p horizon-prepare -- sounds
 cargo run --release -p horizon-client -- --render-distance 12
 ```
 
 Development builds that link quickly: `cargo build --profile fast -p horizon-client`.
 
 | Option | Meaning |
 | --- | --- |
 | `--world NAME` | World folder under `saves/` (default "New World"); reopened if it exists |
 | `--seed N` | Seed for a new world (numbers or text, like vanilla) |
 | `--creative` | Creative mode (instant breaking, pick block) |
 | `--render-distance N` | Chunks, 2..64 (default 12) |
 | `--resources PATH` | Prepared resource directory |
 
 | Control | Action |
 | --- | --- |
 | Mouse | Look (vanilla default sensitivity) |
 | WASD / Space / Left Shift / Left Ctrl | Move, jump, sneak, sprint |
 | Left / right click | Break (hold) / place or use; right click opens crafting tables |
 | Middle click | Pick block (creative) |
 | 1–9, scroll | Select hotbar slot |
 | E | Inventory and 2x2 crafting (shift-click to quick-move or craft all) |
 | Q / Ctrl+Q | Drop one / drop stack |
 | F3 | Debug overlay (position, chunk, light, biome, FPS) |
 | Esc | Pause menu (Save and Quit) |
 
 Worlds autosave every 6000 ticks (5 minutes), when chunks unload and on quit.
 On headless Linux use `vscreen start ./target/release/horizon-client` and
 `vscreen shot`.

 why it has none (`Horizon: no sound: ...`). It opens none with

 listening; `HORIZON_AUDIO=1` opens it there anyway, so send it to a null sink
 (`PIPEWIRE_PROPS='{ target.object=<sink> node.dont-fallback=true }'`). Don't
 mute a test run's stream in the mixer: PipeWire remembers the mute for every
 later `horizon-client`. The launcher starts the game as "Horizon" for that
 reason.
 
 ### Agent control (`horizon-ctl` and MCP)
 
 AI agents and scripts play Horizon through `horizon-ctl`, a command line that
 reads the game as JSON and acts like a player, and `horizon-ctl mcp`, an MCP
 server with the same commands. `--control` makes the game accept them on a
 local socket; under control, losing window focus does not pause the game or
 release held keys, so a script can play while you use other windows.
 
 ```sh
 cargo build --release -p horizon-client --bins
 C=target/release/horizon-ctl
 $C launch --world Survival --seed 5 --wait   # start the game, open or create the world, wait for it
 $C state                                     # player, world, screen, crosshair target
 $C find-block birch_log                      # the 16 nearest loaded logs
 $C goto -0.5 65 -2.5 --near 2.5              # walk there along a path

 $C inventory                                 # hotbar, inventory, armor, offhand, counts
 $C open-inventory                            # craft planks in the 2x2 grid:
 $C click-slot 0; $C click-slot 100 right; $C click-slot 0; $C click-slot 200 shift; $C close
 $C place 2 65 -2 --item birch_planks         # {"changed": true, "block": {...}}
 $C pause; $C ui                              # the pause menu's widgets: ids, kinds, labels, bounds
 $C click options; $C set fov 0.75; $C click done   # widgets by id
 $C screenshot /tmp/view.png                  # PNG of the next presented frame
 $C quit                                      # save and exit
 ```
 
 `horizon-ctl help` lists the commands by group and `horizon-ctl COMMAND --help`
 explains one with examples; `horizon-ctl help --game` lists what the running
 game accepts, test hooks included.
 
 - **Observe:** `state` (position, rotation, velocity, health, food, saturation,
